The AgriCapture Latin America Rice Methane Project will generate emission reductions under VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project supports rice growers in Latin America in adopting improved irrigation practices to reduce both greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and water use. Within the project, growers will implement improved irrigation practices. Prior to project implementation, rice growers in the project practiced continuous flood irrigation. Continuous flooding creates an anaerobic soil environment that fosters methane producing microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). Methane emissions rise as the duration of the flooded period increases, due to the buildup of these microbes (Searchinger & Waite, 2014). By introducing periods of drying that allow oxygen to reenter the soil, improved irrigation practices, like single-drainage and alternate wetting and drying (AWD), can significantly reduce methane emissions. Research indicates that AWD lowers methane emissions by 47% while also decreasing water consumption by up to 39% (Gao, 2024; Atwill R. L., 2020). Participating growers may also transition from transplanted rice to direct seeded rice, another improved irrigation practice. Traditional transplanted rice involves rice seedlings being grown in a nursery before being planted in puddled fields (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). The process requires a prohibitive amount of labor, and puddling the field requires large amounts of irrigation (Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). Additionally, the puddled fields established before planting increases methane emissions due to increasing the period of anaerobic conditions (Reddy, et al., 2025). When compared to transplanted rice, direct seeded rice reduces methane emissions and water consumption by 70% and 8-12% respectively (Reddy, et al., 2025; Ishfaq, Akbar, Anjum, & Anwar-Ijl-Haq, 2020). Rice cultivation in continuously flooded paddy fields, as currently practiced in the project area, is one of the dominant anthropogenic sources of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly methane (CH4) emissions. As rice in India is cultivated primarily by smallholder farmers, it is crucial to address these GHG emissions in a multi-stakeholder program with on-the-ground support. Activities and technologies to reduce GHG emissions must be readily available and implementable for smallholders, considering water shortage and potential soil fertility issues as well as labor constraints in these farming systems. The objective of The Good Rice Alliance improved rice production program in India is to address the methane-intensive method of flooded rice cultivation to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by introducing various agricultural practices that contribute to reducing the anaerobic decomposition of organic matter. The project focuses on transitioning rice farms from the conventional method of continuous flooding to the alternating wetting and drying (AWD) technique. AWD introduces controlled irrigation with periodical flooding and monitoring of the water table to ensure soil aeriation while maintaining optimal water supply to ensure full rice yield. In its initial phase, TGRA involves more than 12,000 smallholder farmers who cultivate more than 16,000 hectares of rice fields with one or two rice growing seasons per year. The program is implemented in collaboration with regional partners in all participating states. The program improves the farmers’ livelihoods by reducing their production costs and improving yield, supported by direct payments for participating in the project. Production efficiency gain, yield increase and water savings provide multiple SDG benefits beyond SDG 13, namely contributions to SDG 2 and SDG 6. The estimated net GHG emission reductions from the project are 181,500 tCO2 equivalent per year, over a crediting period of 10 years.

The AgriCapture Southeast Asia Rice Methane Project will generate emission reductions under VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project supports rice growers in Southeast Asia in adopting improved irrigation practices to reduce both greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and water use. Within the project, growers will implement improved irrigation practices. Prior to project implementation, rice growers in the project practiced continuous flood irrigation.

Respira Patagonia is a high-impact Grouped Project focused on Agricultural Land Management (ALM), situated across the vast and iconic landscapes of the Magallanes and Chilean Antarctica Region, including Tierra del Fuego. Utilizing the VM0042 methodology, the project covers an initial phase of 250,000 hectares dedicated to the transition from conventional extensive grazing to Regenerative Livestock Management.The project is designed to tackle the historical degradation of the Patagonian steppe. By implementing planned grazing and rotational models, Respira Patagonia restores the natural carbon-sink capacity of these grasslands. Over its 20-year crediting period, the project is conservatively estimated to remove approximately 17 million tonnes of $CO_{2}e$ from the atmosphere, making it a cornerstone for regional climate action.Key Impact Pillars:Massive Carbon Removals: Targeted sequestration of ~17M tCO2e through enhanced Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) stocks.Ecosystem Restoration: Active recovery of the fragile Patagonian steppe, reversing desertification and improving water retention.Biodiversity Lifeline: By restoring native grasslands, the project provides a thriving habitat for endemic species, ensuring the conservation of Southern Chile unique biological heritage.Scalable Sustainability: As a Grouped Project, it offers a robust framework for local estancias to join the green economy, fostering resilience for rural communities.Respira Patagonia represents a paradigm shift in Patagonian ranching, proving that profitable livestock production can coexist with large-scale carbon sequestration and the preservation of one of the world’s last wild frontiers.

The Venture Carbon Tropical Agricultural Soil Carbon Removal Project is a grouped initiative developed by Venture Carbon Ltda. under the VCS VM0042 v2.2 methodology and VCS Standard v4.7, targeting measurable increases in soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and reductions in GHG emissions (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O) across consolidated agricultural and grazing lands in Brazil. Classified under Agricultural Land Management (ALM), Sectoral Scope 14 (AFOLU), the project spans a 20-year crediting period (2025–2045) with estimated total removals of approximately 13.9 million tCO₂e. Venture Carbon fully funds every stage of the carbon project lifecycle, from soil sampling and laboratory analysis to certification, third-party audits, credit issuance, and sale, eliminating financial barriers for participating producers. The project is grounded in agronomic science, prioritizing the biological and chemical foundations of productive systems: soil health, microbial biology, and nutrient cycling. By restoring degraded areas and sequestering carbon through improved management practices, including no-till farming, diversified crop rotation, cover cropping, and crop-livestock-forestry integration, the project aligns land recovery with verified carbon removal outcomes. All participating properties must demonstrate full compliance with the Brazilian Forest Code and applicable environmental regulations. Eligibility screening includes geospatial verification through MapBiomas to confirm no native ecosystem conversion occurred within ten years prior to inclusion. As a grouped project, new activity instances may be added over time provided they meet all methodological and regulatory requirements. The project positions Brazilian tropical agriculture as a strategic source of high-integrity, science-based carbon removals in the voluntary carbon market, contributing to multiple Sustainable Development Goals while reinforcing the productive capacity and environmental resilience of participating farms.

The project is an Improved Agricultural Land Management (IALM) initiative implemented under the VM0042 methodology across approximately 20,000 hectares of cropland in Northern Kazakhstan. The project area is primarily used for the cultivation of wheat and sunflower. Under the baseline scenario, agricultural practices consist of conventional crop rotations with fallow periods between cropping seasons. These practices result in exposed soils during non-growing periods, leading to soil organic carbon (SOC) loss, increased erosion, and gradual land degradation. The project introduces cover cropping as the primary intervention, replacing fallow periods with continuous vegetative cover. Cover crops such as winter rye are established following the harvest of the main crop and are not harvested for commercial purposes. Instead, it is terminated prior to the next planting season and incorporated into the soil, contributing to organic matter and improving soil structure. Through these activities, the project enhances carbon sequestration by increasing SOC stocks. Carbon is removed from the atmosphere through plant growth and stored in soils via root biomass and crop residues. Additional benefits include reduced soil erosion, improved moisture retention, and enhanced nutrient cycling. The project is expected to generate greenhouse gas removals primarily from SOC accumulation, with an estimated average of 38,000 tCO₂e per year over the crediting period.

The PRO Carbono Project in Argentina is a science-based, farmer-centered initiative led by Agro Bayer SRL to accelerate the transition toward regenerative agriculture at scale. Structured as a grouped Agricultural Land Management (ALM) program, the project is implemented across Argentina’s main agricultural regions, covering 11 provinces with diverse productive, soil, and climate conditions. Through Bayer’s agribusiness network, digital platforms, and technical support, participating farmers are enabled to adopt improved land management practices, including enhanced crop residue management, more diversified and intensified crop rotations, the integration of cover crops within three-year production cycles, and optimized input application. These interventions are designed to increase soil organic carbon (SOC) stocks and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions while preserving productivity and strengthening farm resilience. By improving year-round soil cover, increasing biomass inputs, and enhancing nutrient-use efficiency, the project generates measurable climate benefits alongside agronomic and environmental co-benefits, such as healthier soils, greater system stability, and improved adaptive capacity under lately climate change scenario. PRO Carbono Argentina combines applied science, digital innovation, and practical farm-level implementation to create a scalable pathway for climate-smart agriculture. Its additionality is supported by the opportunity to tune the baseline and support adoption of regenerative practices in the target regions and by the project’s role in helping growers overcome technical, operational, and financial barriers that often limit broader adoption. As a result, the initiative positions agricultural producers as key contributors to climate mitigation, while reinforcing long-term carbon permanence, sustainable productivity, and the transformation of agricultural landscapes into more resilient and lower-emission production systems.

The project, initiated by Agbiotech (Tokyo, Japan) in active operational collaboration with local partner Subhiksha (Bangalore, Karnataka, India), is a climate-smart agricultural initiative designed to systematically reduce methane emissions from smallholder lowland paddy rice cultivation. The pilot phase encompasses a designated 19.5-hectare footprint situated within the anthropogenically irrigated agricultural plains of the Davanagere district in Karnataka, India. The primary objective of the intervention is to establish a verified, scalable digital Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification framework that demonstrates how structural adjustments to traditional water-delivery and irrigation workflows can successfully suppress soil methanogenesis without compromising smallholder crop yields or food security.

The Agreena Kazakhstan Carbon Project reduces agricultural GHG emissions and increases removals through the implementation of project activities rooted in the central principles of regenerative agriculture. The Project intends to support farmers across the northern Kazakhstan grain belt in transitioning to regenerative agriculture by adopting sustainable management practices that maintain yields while ensuring the long-term viability of their land. The technologies and activities to be implemented by project participants, either individually or as a combined suite of practices.

Khentii Sustainable Grassland Management Project (hereafter as ‘the project’) is located in Khentii Province of Mongolia. The project is aimed to restore the local degraded grassland ecosystem from adoption of sustainable grassland management practices, such as implementing systematic seasonal pasture rotations, limiting the timing and number of grazing animals on degraded pastures, and providing regular training to herders on sustainable grazing practices. The project proponent is Anhe Carbon Industry Limited.

This Malaysian Paddy dMRV Program seeks to implement improved rice cultivation practices in Malaysia under Verra’s VCS Methodology VM0051: Improved Management in Rice Production Systems. The project will primarily reduce methane emissions by transitioning rice fields from continuous flooding to Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD), supported by an agronomist-approved standard operation procedure and a smart farming digital monitoring system to guide the periodic drainage and re-irrigation based on field water thresholds. The resulting soil aeration from the draining and drying of rice fields interrupts the anaerobic conditions that support methane production, while improving water-use efficiency and maintaining rice yields. Where agronomically suitable, participating farmers may also optimise and reduce nitrogen fertiliser application through soil profiling and nutrient planning, thereby reducing nitrous oxide emissions associated with surplus nitrogen inputs. The project is being developed as a grouped project across multiple eligible locations within Malaysia with a minimum renewable five-year crediting period. Additional activity instances are to be included to the project gradually as participation expands from initial project instance (district level) to state and national scale. Project areas will be located within established rice cultivation zones across Peninsular Malaysia, with a projected participation scale of 100,000 hectares over the first five years of crediting period. The AgriCapture Improved Grazing Project (the “Project”) is a grouped project that implements planned rotational grazing on grazing land in the United States. The first monitoring period includes one project activity instance on approximately 6,634 acres of privately owned grazing land in southwestern Montana, in the area of the Bridger Mountain Range and the Crazy Mountains. The Project’s baseline scenario is continuous grazing, in which cattle graze freely within large pastures for extended, indefinite periods before being moved. Under the Project, ranch managers implement an improved grazing plan that increases livestock stock density and the frequency of pasture rotation relative to the baseline. These practices, commonly referred to as rotational grazing, adaptive multi-paddock (AMP) grazing, or management-intensive grazing (MiG), have been shown to increase the rate of soil carbon sequestration in grassland soils, generating removals over the Project crediting period. The Project start date is 01-September-2023, and the first crediting period runs through 30-August-2043. Average annual estimated GHG emission reductions and removals (ERRs) for the first crediting period are 1,990 tCO₂e, with total estimated ERRs of 23,800 tCO₂e over the 20-year period.
